endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Confidentiality protections typically need to specify that identifying information will not be shared with the AI vendor during rootcause analysis, since vendor contracts often create indirect channels back to a reporter's employer.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether protecting reporter identity or publishing plain-language data-handling notices increases AI incident reporting, and none documents the reporter-exposure hazard directly. The recommendation currently rests on a single framework endorsement from CHAI governance playbooks.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The CHAI playbook statement is expert guidance and does not substitute for comparative data on reporting rates or reporter outcomes.

The only supporting source is a voluntary framework using "should" language. It specifies that identifying information be withheld from AI vendors during root-cause analysis because vendor contracts may create indirect channels back to a reporter's employer. No supplied study examines how this contractual pathway operates in practice.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI incident reporting volume, reporting quality, and reporter retaliation or exposure events before and after organizations adopt confidentiality protections, vendor data-sharing restrictions, and plain-language notices. Such studies should also measure whether staff read and understand the notices.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers staff or patients in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Whether plain-language notices reach staff with limited English proficiency or lower literacy, or whether safety-net systems can fund confidential reporting channels, remains unknown.
